newsitem.title: USA: Most U.S. debt futures finish rangebound day lower.
newsitem.headline: Most U.S. debt futures finish rangebound day lower.

text.p: Most U.S. debt futures finished a rangebound day slightly lower due to nervousness that the Federal Reserve may offer yet more clues on the direction of monetary policy, traders and analysts said.

"People are changing their opinions daily on the perceived odds of a rate hike by the Fed," one Eurodollar futures trader said. "The market has flip-flopped so much in the last two weeks on rumor and innuendo."
Traders and dealers were still smarting from comments reported by Reuters on Tuesday that eight out of 12 Fed banks submitted requests for a discount rate hike.
Three out of the eight banks favored a 50-basis-point discount rate hike, the senior official said.

Before pit trade opened on Wednesday, one news wire service quoted an anonymous Fed source saying that while retail sales and consumer prices were lower than expected in August, there are still inflation risks. The comments put marginal pressure on bonds and Eurodollars, traders said.

"I believe the Fed orchestrated this as way to to force a tightening," a floor trader said. "It shows a distinctive riff within the Fed between those who want to tighten and those who -- for political reasons -- want steady-as-she-goes."
Another trader speculated that the Fed released the information as a way to prepare the market for a possible hike in U.S. rates at Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
"They are massaging the market," he said. "We've seen them do this before when the market has gotten a little too complacent."

James Annable, chief economist at First Chicago NBD Corporation, said he believes the Federal Reserve was surprised by the bond market's positive response to the August Consumer Price Index (CPI) and retail sales data.
"The Fed would much rather the market speculate between a 25- and 50-basis-point increase, than price in a zero chance for a rate hike," Annable said.
After Tuesday's sharp decline, traders said both T-bond and Eurodollar futures were now fairly priced for at least a 25-basis-point tightening next week.
"The yield (on the 30-year cash bond) is at seven percent," one trader said. "We're at ground-zero, and until we get a really good reason, we are not going to break out of this range."
December Eurodollars traded near the 94.00 level, which would translate into another 50-basis-point hike by the end of the year.

At the end of pit trade, December bonds were off 02/32 at 108-02/32, 10-year notes were off 03/32 at 106-15/32, December and March Eurodollars were unchanged at 94.07 and 93.91, and March T-bills were off one basis point at 94.47. Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuter.com
